extracted.intended_audience: literary scholars, narratology students, and advanced creative-writing theorists
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and analyze the narrative devices that govern frequency/iteration (how often events recur, how series are bounded, diversified, and integrated with singulative events) in prose fiction; reconstruct hidden temporal structures that shape a text's iteration. Useful for narratological analysis or for crafting iterative narrative sections in fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination (diachronic limits of a series)
rubrics_metrics.description: The diachronic limits of a series can be left implicit or made definite; novelistic narration generally indicates a series' beginning and end, but determination can be absolute (dates) or by reference to a singular event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether a recurrent series in the text has explicit start/end markers or remains indefinite (e.g., 'After a certain year we never saw...'). Determination can also punctuate stages of a series, dividing it into subseries (before/after a singular event). Example: the breach between Swann and the Verdurins ends one series of meetings and inaugurates another. Scoring note: a well-handled determination clarifies temporal boundaries or deliberately leaves them vague for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification (frequency — definite vs. indefinite)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequency can be specified indefinitely (sometimes, certain days) or definitely (every day, every Sunday); specifications can be simple (every Saturday) or complex (combinations/embedded laws of recurrence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify frequency locutions as indefinite (flexible, permitting variation) or definite (regular, law-like). Use of adverbs ('sometimes,' 'often') produces flexible variation; use of absolutes ('every day') produces strong rhythmic expectation. Examples: Combray's mix of 'every day', 'every Saturday', and 'every year between Easter and October.' Evaluate how specification structures reader expectations and narrative rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex / hierarchical specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or several laws of recurrence can be superimposed, producing compound or hierarchical specifications (e.g., 'every Saturday in the month of May'; overarching rules governing subordinate specifications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect and map superimposed recurrence laws and their hierarchy (local vs. overarching specifications). Example: Combray's iterative specifications (every day / every Saturday / every year between Easter and October). Complex specifications enable multilayered patterns of variation; reconstruct them to reveal the text's temporal skeleton.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension (duration of the iterative unit)
rubrics_metrics.description: An iterative unit's duration affects its narrative potential: very short units yield little room for expansion (pinpointed), while extended units can be expanded into full narrative sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the chosen iterative unit (e.g., 'every evening I go to bed early' vs. 'a sleepless night' or 'Sunday at Combray') affords narrative expansion. Anti-pattern: retaining only invariant features reduces the text to a diagrammatic timetable. Good practice: choose units with enough extent to permit variation and scene-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal determination (singulative interposition creating subseries)
rubrics_metrics.description: A singular event interposed into an iterative series can function to determine the series internally, producing subseries (before/after variants) and changing behaviour within the series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify singular events that subdivide a recurring series into diachronically sequenced variants (e.g., before/after the Lady in pink). Distinguish determinative singulative events (which produce lasting change) from mere illustrative or exceptional anecdotes that leave the series unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal specification (iterative diversification by alternation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal specification subdivides a recurrence into alternating variants (not successive subseries but alternating classes), producing iterative diversification without singulative change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for alternation patterns that partition a recurrence (e.g., 'one day out of two', 'good weather/bad weather' ordering of walks). These specifications create iterative variants that alternate rather than succeed diachronically. Example: Meseglise vs. Guermantes way alternation in Combray. Evaluate how alternation produces textual variety while retaining iterative mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concretization/diversification techniques (preventing diagrammatic barrenness)
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid the 'diagrammatic barrenness' of listing invariants, narratives use internal determinations and specifications (and other devices) to 'concretize' iterations and diversify portrayal of repeated units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the text employs internal determinations, internal specifications, embedded examples, or descriptive detail to flesh out iterative units. Example anti-pattern: a fixed timetable like 'to bed at nine, read an hour...' which lacks narrative interest. Effective practice: introduce internal variations, embedded scenes, or focal detail to make each recurrence engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-iterative convention
rubrics_metrics.description: When iterative diversification is exhausted, the writer may use the convention of the pseudo-iterative — singulative language/form used to evoke repetition or to stand in for iteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize pseudo-iterative uses where a single, singulative formulation implies a habitual recurrence. Evaluate whether this device serves to suggest iteration while allowing narrative focus on an instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singulative used as illustration or exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Singulative events may be invoked either as literal illustrations/confirmations of an iterative law (positive function) or as exceptions/deviations from it (negative function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate illustrative singulatives (e.g., 'Thus one day Albertine ...' exemplifying the iterative law) from exceptional singulatives (e.g., 'Once, however ...' as a deviation). Examples: steeples of Martinville (exception) vs. Albertine episode (illustration). Analyze how the singulative's function reinforces or transgresses the iterative code.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal and External Diachrony (aging vs. timeless iteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Iterative units can be narrated without reference to external chronological change (timeless reiteration), or they can integrate external diachrony — irreversible transformations across years (deaths, maturation) that alter the iterated unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the narrative treats iterations as invariant types or as historically changing (aging, maturation, losses). Example: Combray II treats walks with respect to day, season, and years; external diachrony introduces irreversible transformations that intersect with internal iterative structure. Evaluate how the interplay of internal and external diachronies shapes meaning and character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternation and Transitions (iterative/singulative relations and subordination)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative rhythm may be governed by alternation between iterative and singulative modes rather than by classical summary/scene alternation; relations include iterative sections subordinated to singulative scenes and vice versa, and complex nested combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map functional subordinations (e.g., an iterative descriptive passage inserted into a singulative scene, or a singulative scene illustrating an iterative sequence). Look for nested structures where a singulative episode calls up an iterative parenthesis or where an iterative development is itself subordinated to a singulative anchor. Examples: Guermantes' wit (iterative description within a dinner scene); steeples of Martinville (singulative within iterative walks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative as temporal mode (frequentative tense and lexical markers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The iterative is a temporal aspect often signalled by frequentative tenses and lexical markers (e.g., 'now', 'thenceforth', 'had become'), which present states as successive substitutions rather than causally linked events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to tense/aspect and lexical signals that create a frequentative mode (lists of 'now' occurrences, repeated 'every evening...' constructions). This mode often expresses forgetting, substitution of states, and a lack of perceived continuity. Evaluate how aspect choices contribute to the narrative's temporal effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic reconstruction / schematization of hidden temporal structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative analysis should aim to reveal the 'immanent' temporal structures (the hidden skeleton of determinations/specifications/alternations) beneath surface stylistic manifestation, often by schematizing the iterative system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconstruct the underlying temporal diagram (e.g., mapping spring/summer/rare variants for 'returns home') to explain why the text's surface continuity depends on a complex, often tangled hierarchy of recurrence laws. Note: the schematization's purpose is explanatory (foundations of the text), not aesthetic judgement of style.
